html:
Lawrence Kohlberg extended Piaget’s work into the moral domain. He asked not what moral choices people make but why-probing the reasoning that underlies judgments in moral dilemmas (e.g., Heinz stealing a drug to save his wife). Analyzing thousands of interviews, he traced a universal developmental sequence with three progressively broader frames of reference, each containing two qualitatively distinct stages. Advancement depends less on age than on sustained cognitive conflict, education, and social perspective-taking; most adults consolidate in the middle levels, and only a minority reach the highest, fully principled orientation.

Stages

Pre-conventional Level (self-focused logic).

Stage 1 - Obedience & Punishment. Right and wrong are tied to concrete consequences delivered by authorities. The child’s question is "Will I be punished?" rather than "Is it just?" Rules are fixed, external dictates; moral action equals literal compliance.

Stage 2 - Instrumental Exchange. Morality becomes a pragmatic reciprocity: "You scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours." Actions are right if they satisfy one’s own needs or, transactionally, another’s ("Heinz should steal the drug because he’ll be happier if his wife lives"). Perspective-taking is present but strictly strategic, and standards remain essentially personal.

Conventional Level (group-focused logic).

Stage 3 - Interpersonal Accord & Conformity. The good-boy/good-girl stance centers on living up to expectations of close others. Intentions, loyalty, and maintaining relationships matter more than tangible outcomes. The self is defined by perceived social roles; shame, not guilt, polices behavior.

Stage 4 - Social-Order Maintaining. Reasoning widens to society at large: laws, duty, and institutional authority preserve the collective. Morality equals doing one’s duty and respecting the social system (e.g., Heinz must obey the law even if it seems unfair). Most adults stabilize here, where order and predictability outweigh individual contingencies.

Post-conventional (principle-focused logic).

Stage 5 - Social Contract. People recognize that laws are social contracts created for mutual benefit and therefore revocable when they violate fundamental rights. Moral reasoning weighs legal statutes against broader values like liberty or life, endorsing civil disobedience if a law is unjust. The individual can imagine an ideal society and judge the actual one against it.

Stage 6 - Universal Ethical Principles. At this rare pinnacle, justice is anchored in self-chosen, logically consistent principles (equality, human dignity) that hold irrespective of majority will or statute. Moral obligation stems from an internalized sense of universalizable duty; the person would act the same way if roles were reversed or scrutiny absent. Gandhi’s or King’s willingness to suffer for an inclusive moral vision exemplifies this stage.

Kohlberg argued that each stage reorganizes the very structure of moral thought; one cannot "skip" stages because each provides the cognitive scaffolding for the next. Yet critics note cultural biases toward individualist, justice-centered reasoning and question whether moral development is as linear as the model suggests. Still, the framework illuminates how the locus of moral authority can migrate from external control, to communal norms, to principled self-legislation-echoing other developmental theories that chart the expansion of perspective and agency across the human lifespan.
